title: A Cabinet Full of Roy Cohns
gist: Reviewing two new books, the piece argues Trump's second-term abuses trace directly to his 1970s mentor Roy Cohn, whose playbook of relentless lying, enemy-targeting, and never apologizing now animates a cabinet of obsequious loyalists who have turned the DOJ into Trump's personal law firm and are reviving a Red Scare against Democrats.

insights.claim: Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark's book American Scoundrel argues most of Trump's political tactics came from Roy Cohn's playbook: lie relentlessly, never admit error, threaten enemies and press, never leave a paper trail, and always counterattack by accusing the accuser.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A reusable behavioral model for anticipating Trump's tactics—deny, counterattack, never apologize—useful for gaming out policy and political confrontations.
insights.quote: lie to the public relentlessly and without fear of contradiction; deny unflattering facts and drown them out with strident counterclaims; never admit error or defeat

insights.claim: In contrast to his first term, Trump's second-term cabinet is filled with obsequious loyalists willing to promote any lie, target any enemy, and break any law he desires, per Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan's book Regime Change.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A loyalist-purged executive removes internal guardrails, raising the odds of unchecked, norm-breaking policy actions—an institutional-risk signal for markets and rule of law.
insights.quote: Trump has filled his cabinet with slavishly obsequious loyalists
insights.locator: In contrast to his first term

insights.claim: Trump's first-term officials who questioned him—Jeff Sessions, John Kelly, H.R. McMaster, Rex Tillerson, and Mark Esper—were fired, and in the second term he sidelined anyone who had ever second-guessed him, with even praising Mike Pence after Jan. 6 grounds for exile.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: The systematic purge of independent-minded officials documents a shift from a constrained to an unconstrained executive.
insights.quote: Even the slightest deviation from Trump’s first-term liturgy—especially the outright lie that he won the 2020 election—was grounds for exile in the second term.
insights.locator: In his second term, Trump solved this problem

insights.claim: In August, Trump got his personal attorney Todd Blanche confirmed as attorney general, positioning a loyalist willing to harass and prosecute Trump's political enemies, after filling senior DOJ ranks with devoted loyalists and turning its leadership into 'his personal law firm.'
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Politicization of the DOJ shatters its post-Watergate independence, a material erosion of legal-institutional predictability that raises rule-of-law risk.
insights.quote: effectively turning the DoJ leadership into his personal law firm
insights.locator: And nothing was more important to the new president

insights.claim: Trump publicly pressed for indictments of political enemies including former FBI Director James Comey, Sen. Adam Schiff, and NY Attorney General Letitia James, saying of James 'I want to make her life miserable' and that it didn't matter whether the charges were true.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Openly retaliatory prosecution of named adversaries signals politicized enforcement risk that could extend to businesses and individuals seen as opponents.
insights.quote: I want to make her life miserable
insights.locator: Trump, again echoing the tactics of his mentor Cohn

insights.claim: The review argues Cohn's tactics failed with McCarthy in the 1950s but succeeded with Trump because society is now gripped by deep existential fear and a 'longing for the past'—rooted in the failures of globalization, 9/11, the Iraq War, and widening inequality—that demagogues can manipulate.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Frames the durability of Trumpism as structural, not personal—implying elevated populist-driven political risk persists regardless of any single leader.
insights.quote: societal fear, which “leaders can manipulate into a sense of existential threat”

insights.claim: A key factor making Trump more successful than McCarthy is that he captured the capital-owning economic establishment, echoing how Cohn cultivated the very rich in New York—George Steinbrenner, Rupert Murdoch, Si Newhouse, Ronald Perelman—as part of his 'favor bank.'
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Elite/capital-class buy-in is what gives Trumpism staying power over McCarthyism—signaling business establishment alignment rather than resistance.
insights.quote: He has also captured the capital-owning class—the economic establishment—in a way McCarthy never did.
insights.locator: One factor that may have made Trump more successful

insights.claim: Biographer Kai Bird argues McCarthyism never failed but survived because Eisenhower and the establishment never stood up to it—just as the Republican Party is not standing up to Trump today—making the Cohn 'dark side of America' a recurring pattern.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: The thesis that elite non-resistance perpetuates demagoguery implies durable political dysfunction absent institutional pushback.
insights.quote: Roy’s story is the dark side of America—a story that keeps repeating itself.
insights.locator: In an email to Foreign Policy, Bird said

insights.claim: Trump and his team are reviving the Red Scare, resurrecting anti-communist labels to tar all Democrats—centrist or socialist—echoing Hofstadter's observation that for McCarthyism 'Communism was not the target but the weapon.'
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A revived Red Scare framing signals escalating partisan delegitimization that raises domestic political-polarization risk.
insights.quote: Trump and his team are now targeting “communism” again, resurrecting the Red Scare
insights.locator: In a disturbing closing of the circle
